\subsection{Conformal Prediction in Robotics}

Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees and has been applied to robotic safety and planning.
ACP-CBF~\cite{zhou2025acp_cbf} uses adaptive conformal prediction to construct control barrier functions for safe RL under distribution shift.
CPLoop~\cite{wang2025cploop} integrates CP-based uncertainty into trajectory optimization as feedback constraints.
Conformalized Teleoperation~\cite{zhao2024conformalized} applies CP to calibrate confidence regions when mapping human inputs to high-dimensional robot actions.
Our work uses conformal prediction scores as conditioning features for a learned correction module, rather than as safety constraints. We find that at the $K{=}10$ sample budget, CP-derived features do not improve closed-loop performance over observation-only conditioning (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}).

\subsection{Inference-Time Compute Scaling}

Test-time compute scaling improves language model outputs through best-of-N sampling with verifiers~\cite{snell2024scaling}, reward models as test-time verifiers~\cite{dai2025rover}, or decision-aware sample weighting~\cite{chun2025dasip}.
Our pipeline transfers multi-sample generation to embodied action spaces, drawing $K{=}10$ samples and selecting via $L_2$ argmin.
Our component decomposition reveals that learned correction is the active mechanism while multi-sampling provides the centered starting point that correction requires (Section~\ref{sec:main_results}).

% --- Para 1: VLAs are impressive but fragile under distribution shift ---
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) that generate actions via flow matching~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla,lipman2023flow} have reached near-saturation on in-distribution benchmarks such as LIBERO~\cite{liu2023libero}.
Yet this performance masks severe fragility: visual and physical perturbations common in deployment (camera viewpoint shifts, object layout changes, robot initial-state variation) routinely degrade success by over 65 percentage points.
On the LIBERO+ benchmark~\cite{fei2025liberoplus}, $\pi_0$ drops from 94.2\% to 6.6\% under initial-state perturbation, and UniVLA drops from 95.2\% to 4.3\% under viewpoint changes.
Closing this robustness gap without retraining the base policy is a prerequisite for deploying VLAs outside tightly controlled laboratory settings.

4	Deploying a pretrained Vision-Language-Action model (VLA) on a new task or environment typically requires fine-tuning on task-specific demonstrations, yet collecting such data is expensive and the resulting checkpoint may not generalize further.
5	An alternative is to treat the VLA as a frozen action prior and improve its outputs at inference time.
6	Flow-matching VLAs~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla,lipman2023flow} are natural candidates: each forward pass produces a stochastic action sample, so drawing multiple samples opens the door to selection and correction without modifying model weights.
7	The question is how to use these samples effectively.
8	
9	% --- Para 2: Existing approaches and the gap ---
10	Two lines of work address this challenge.
11	Training-time methods improve the base policy through robustness-aware objectives~\cite{srpo2025,robustvla2025,digflow2025} or test-time reinforcement learning~\cite{liu2026ttvla}, but require retraining or per-task RL and remain bounded by the training distribution.
12	Inference-time methods leave the policy frozen: ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} applies conformal quantile regression for uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution detection, but does not learn corrective residuals; A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} trains a per-step correction head on frozen VLA action chunks, but applies correction unconditionally without multi-sample selection or explicit magnitude control; VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} applies evolutionary optimization over action samples, but incurs 2.41\,s per control step.
13	Despite growing interest in inference-time action refinement, fundamental design questions remain unanswered: how much does selection contribute relative to correction, what features should condition the correction module, and how sensitive is performance to correction magnitude?

\section*{AI Disclosure}

AI tools (Claude, GitHub Copilot) were used to assist with code development and manuscript drafting. All experimental results, analyses, and scientific claims were verified by the authors.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a sample-select-correct pipeline that wraps a frozen flow-matching VLA with $L_2$ argmin selection and a lightweight CRM (${\sim}$327K parameters).
On LIBERO-Object, the pipeline achieves $17.6 \pm 2.6$\% versus $11.6 \pm 1.1$\% for VLA-only ($p = 0.003$, Mann-Whitney U), with a +5.3\,pp margin over argmin selection ($p = 0.014$).
In contrast to LLM test-time scaling~\cite{snell2024scaling}, where selection among candidates drives improvement, our decomposition reveals that in low-dimensional continuous action spaces selection alone provides no benefit: learned correction is the active mechanism, but multi-sampling is an enabling condition ($K{=}1$ correction alone: 10.3\%, selection without correction: 11.7\%).
Per-DOF conformal features do not improve over observation-only conditioning at $K{=}10$, establishing feature choice as a critical design factor.
On LIBERO-Spatial, correction provides no benefit, bounding the scope to object-centric manipulation where errors are correctable at the action level.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
All experiments use LIBERO in simulation; real-robot transfer is untested.
We evaluate only SmolVLA (450M); transfer to larger VLAs is unknown.
Per-seed variance is substantial (margins range from $-1$ to $+10$\,pp); 17.6\% mean success is far from deployment-ready.
A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} reports 67--72\% by training SmolVLA from scratch on LIBERO, but their setting (full training) differs fundamentally from ours (frozen checkpoint, 11.6\% baseline).

\paragraph{Inference-time scaling with $K$.}
The correction benefit concentrates in the transition from $K{=}1$ to $K{=}5$: $K{=}1$ (10.3\%, 3 seeds) $\to$ $K{=}5$ (16.3\%, 4 seeds) $\to$ $K{=}10$ (17.6\%, 7 seeds). The main jump is $K{=}1{\to}K{=}5$ (+5.95\,pp), with diminishing returns from $K{=}5{\to}K{=}10$ (+1.35\,pp). All three settings use the same CRM trained on $K{=}10$ argmin-selected data; only inference-time $K$ varies. At $K{=}1$, the CRM falls below the VLA-only baseline (10.3\% vs.\ 11.6\%), likely because the single sample lacks argmin centering and shifts outside the CRM's training distribution. $K{=}5$ captures ${\sim}$82\% of the correction benefit at half the compute, suggesting a practical sweet spot. Full analysis in Appendix~\ref{sec:k_scaling}.

\paragraph{Object benchmark: correction helps.}
On LIBERO-Object, obs\_only at $\varepsilon{=}0.1$ achieves 16.2\% (6 seeds), and at $\varepsilon{=}0.2$ achieves $17.6 \pm 2.6$\% (7 seeds).
Across seven seeds ($\varepsilon{=}0.2$), the pipeline achieves mean $17.6 \pm 2.6$\%, versus VLA-only mean $11.6 \pm 1.1$\% (+6.0\,pp, $p = 0.003$, Mann-Whitney U) and Argmin mean $12.3 \pm 2.6$\% (+5.3\,pp, $p = 0.014$).

At seed 42, all three baselines achieve 12.0\%: neither averaging nor selection alone helps, confirming that action diversity does not center around the correct action.
The obs\_only CRM breaks through this plateau by predicting corrective residuals conditioned on the observation embedding.

\paragraph{Pipeline decomposition.}

1	Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation degrade under distribution shift, yet improving their performance without retraining remains underexplored.
2	We propose a sample-select-correct pipeline for inference-time action refinement of frozen flow-matching VLAs that draws multiple action samples, selects the most representative candidate via $L_2$ argmin, and applies a learned residual correction bounded in magnitude.
3	The correction module is a ${\sim}$327K-parameter MLP conditioned on the frozen VLA's observation embedding, trained offline with supervised $L_2$ loss on demonstration data.

6	A conditioning study demonstrates that feature choice is a critical design factor: observation features produce robust corrections across all tested magnitude bounds (14.3--17.6\%), while per-DOF conformal uncertainty features cause progressive collapse (14\% to 0\%) under the same architecture and training.
7	We further show that multi-sample correction requires stochastic action diversity: tokenized VLAs produce near-identical samples. This establishes an architectural applicability boundary.

\paragraph{Task-specificity of learned corrections.}
A leave-task-out (LTO) evaluation, where the CRM is trained on 15 tasks and evaluated on 5 held-out tasks, yields 2\% success versus 14\% for VLA-only on the held-out set. The CRM actively degrades performance on unseen tasks, indicating that learned corrections are task-specific rather than general-purpose: the module memorizes correction patterns tied to the calibration data distribution.
All results in Table~\ref{tab:main} are in-distribution (the CRM training set covers all 20 LIBERO tasks).
This finding bounds the deployment model: the CRM must be calibrated on data representative of the target task distribution, analogous to how conformal prediction requires exchangeable calibration data.
For an analysis paper, this is a mechanism insight: correction quality is bounded by calibration data coverage, and the pipeline does not provide zero-shot task generalization.
